thread.title: 1978 Nomad Trailer Restoration/Project: 88GMCtruck is at it again.
thread.first_post_html:
Well, I'm up to another project yet again.

Here we have my newest driveway edition: a 1978 Nomad 16' travel trailer. It has a full bath, full kitchen, dinette, couch/bed, and bunk. It has a very nice and open floorplan.
Click this bar to view the full image.

Click this bar to view the full image.


I picked this up just outside of town for a whopping $250. It's been unlicenced/unused since 2003.

The good: It's in good shape outside, just needs a good pressure washing. Inside, all the fabric, fixtures, counters, appliances etc are in great condition. Everything works great.

The bad: Outside, the lights don't all work yet, but that should just be a cleaning/ground issue. the tires look to be original, as they are GoodYear 7.75-15ST tires and have LARGE cracks all over. Inside is going to take the most effort. The subfloor is toast. Stupid trailer manufacturer decided to use chip board for a floor, that crumbles with any moisture. The roof is solid, but part of the paneling inside needs replaced. One small portion of wall needs replaced as well due to some water damage. The roof obviously needs sealed.

So yeah. It's a project. The goal is to have a nice, reliable camper that I can hitch up the truck to and just take off for the weekend. I'll be towing this with the 88 primarily. So, here is the list of items that will be done to the truck and trailer

Truck:
- re-install brake controller
- buy weight distributing hitch
- buy towing mirrors
- install relay and wiring for trailer lights. I've had too many dash light switches burn out on me
- possibly install my 3/4ton springs, or re-install my helper bags with some quick disconnect
- re-gear truck to 4.56s or 4.88s. This one has been in the works awhile now anyway

Trailer:
- replace subfloor, roof skin and partial wall skin
- replace tires and inspect/replace wheel bearings and brakes
- re-seal roof and windows
- fix exterior lighting, possibly replace with LED at some point
- obvious clean and sanitize insides, fridge and water tank
- thinking about re-painting the sides something a little more modern, maybe to match the truck

So anyway, I'll be updating this as I go along, with my budget trailer resto.

I redid an '84 Scotty a couple of years back before I got mad at it and sold it and bought a new Jayco 32 BHDS. I tow it with my '99 1500 ECSB Z71. I bought a set of 3/4 springs for it. It helped it quite a bit while towing.

We installed a new subfloor because part of it in the bathroom was gone, but the joists were good, new hardwood laminate flooring, now countertop, new range hood, water heater, all faucets, interior lights, roof vents, rebuilt both doors (new wood & plastic inside/out), painted the ceiling, bumper, and tongue. It already had a new residental fridge in it that my aunt & uncle had installed. Also resealed the roof seams and then coated the entire roof. When I went to install the water heater, I saw more damage than I was expecting and decided I was done having fun. Decided my last mod was going to be a For Sale sign.

Anyway, I bought most of my stuff from here: http://www.rvpartscenter.com/DeptSelect.asp?SID=50 They typically had the best price. Also bought some from here: http://www.adventurerv.net/ and here: http://www.dyersonline.com/ I've also purchased from http://www.pplmotorhomes.com/parts/r...ccessories.htm

As far as lights go, I found the best/cheapest place to get LED lights was Wal-Mart. I installed those on the camper and they were nice and bright and had no issues. I've bought some more there for our stock trailer and they are also nice and bright with no issues. About $7 - 8 each.

Good luck, and keep us posted.

Thanks for the links, I've already been on adventurerv.net looking at stuff, not sure what I will entirely need but yeah, a few things here and there. Sounds like you have a similar project as I do, hopefully I won't get tired of it or find any bad, hidden damage.

Anyway, I found a free set of radials that will fit it. They are off a Subaru and are the correct metric equivalent (205/70R15) to the tires on it now (7.75-15ST). I know they aren't "trailer" tires, but they are radials and are of higher weight rating than the tires on it now. They will hold me over so I can at least tow it for the time being, until I can buy trailer or light truck tires.

Anyway, I snapped a few more picts of her, after making the 8 mile trip down a gravel road to rest in my yard.
Click this bar to view the full image.

Click this bar to view the full image.

Click this bar to view the full image.


Few inside picts.

Click this bar to view the full image.


The best part. AM/FM and 8-Track! I'm thinking that we are going replace this with a CD player....
Click this bar to view the full image.


I did get a bit of the floor pulled back. Luckily the framing for the floor is still fine. I'm going to add some additional framing in the areas where the foot traffic is also.

Thinking in terms of insurance, because that's what I do, if you ever want to insure it, most all companies will not let you insure it for an agreed price like you can a classic of customized car or truck. Don't put too much money in it or you'll end up with way too much invested for what it's actually worth and insurable for.

I didn't even insure my old Scotty. Spoke to my ins. agent. Agreed that its value wasn't worth insuring and from a liability standpoint, my truck insure would cover it. Now the new Jayco has full coverage.

Yeah, as far as insurance goes, it won't be insured, maybe once it's completed depending on how much it costs. The trailer doesn't book for much so I'm not really worried about it anyway.

Anyway, here is the update. Yesterday I pressure washed the entire trailer. Looks better now. There is a few panels that will need painted as the paint is gone from sun. All the light lenses were pulled and cleaned as well, only one broken lens in all.
Click this bar to view the full image.


Then, I moved inside for a bit. Got the couch/bed out, fresh water tank and water heater pulled. Both seem to be in good condition. I'm going to pour about a gallon of bleach in the water tank and let it sit in the sun for the next few weeks. The good news is thus far, the places I can see structural wood are still solid, only the cheap chip board subfloor and some paneling seems to be bad.

Today, I picked up a set of Republic Enterprise 205/70R15 tires for free. They are in great shape, probably about 60% tread. They actually hold about 150lbs more per tire as well, which is nice. The tires came mounted on a set of Subaru wheels, but the guy wanted to keep them for a rally car he was building. So anyway, with the help of Devin (83GMCK2500) we did the redneck dismount and mount of tires. Used a piece of large lumber and a truck to break the beads and pry bars to mount/dismount the wheels. All went rather easily and they are in the truck, ready for balancing.
Click this bar to view the full image.
cool project man. Good progress so far, keep us updated ! :)

One thing I forgot to mention. We found a few things on e-bay. I think the range hood came from there. We were able to get it really cheap - it was new for like less than $20 including S&H. Heck, I would have that much in spray paint and sand paper for the old one. :)

The bearings also looked great, and the grease appeared as if it had very few miles on it.

Trailer condition before restoration:
- Good exterior with minor cleaning required
- Excellent interior fabric and fixtures, with functional kitchen appliances and a full bath
- Subfloor made of chipboard prone to moisture damage; roof needs sealing
- Some partial wall and paneling replacements needed due to water damage

Restoration progress updates include:
- Replaced trailer subfloor and roofing materials
- Installed new tires and inspected/replaced wheel bearings and brakes
- Cleaned, sanitized interior, including fridge and water tank
- Repaired exterior lighting; considering LED upgrades in the future
- Completed significant flooring work with additional bracing and insulation added
- Plans to install a weight-distributing hitch for better towing performance

post_rewrites.rewritten_content:
I'm currently working on another project: a 1978 Nomad 16' travel trailer. It features a full bath, kitchen, dinette, couch/bed, and bunk, with an open floorplan. I acquired it for $250 and found it unlicensed and unused since 2003.

Pros:
- Good exterior condition; needs pressure washing
- Excellent interior condition: all fabrics, fixtures, counters, and appliances work

Cons:
- Exterior lights need cleaning or grounding
- Original tires have large cracks, likely original
- Subfloor is damaged due to moisture
- Some roof paneling and a section of wall require replacement
- Roof needs sealing
- Interior requires thorough cleaning and sanitization

Towing truck (1988):
- Reinstall brake controller
- Install weight distributing hitch and towing mirrors
- Add relay and wiring for trailer lights
- Consider installing 3/4-ton springs or re-installing helper bags with quick disconnect
- Gear the truck to either 4.56s or 4.88s

Trailer work:
- Replace subfloor, roof skin, and part of the wall
- Replace tires and inspect/replacing wheel bearings and brakes
- Re-seal roof and windows
- Fix exterior lighting; possibly replace with LED later
- Clean and sanitize inside, including fridge and water tank
- Consider repainting the sides for a more modern look

I'll update this as I progress with my budget trailer restoration.

I recently completed a restoration of an '84 Scotty recreational vehicle before selling it to purchase a new Jayco 32 BHDS. I towed it with my '99 1500 ECSB Z71 truck and added 3/4-inch springs for better towing performance. Key modifications included replacing the subfloor in the bathroom, installing hardwood laminate flooring, countertops, a range hood, water heater, faucets, interior lights, roof vents, and rebuilt both doors with new wood and plastic. The ceiling, bumper, and tongue were also painted. A new residential fridge was already installed by my aunt and uncle.

During installation of the water heater, more damage than anticipated was found, leading me to decide against further modifications. My last project was painting a "For Sale" sign for the RV.

Most parts were sourced from http://www.rvpartscenter.com/, which offered competitive pricing. Additional items came from http://www.adventurerv.net/ and http://www.dyersonline.com/. LED lights, installed from Wal-Mart, provided bright, reliable illumination at a cost of $7-8 each.

Thanks for the links; I've checked out adventurerv.net and found a few relevant resources, though I’m not sure what I’ll need entirely just yet. The project seems similar to mine, so hopefully, it won’t bore me or reveal any hidden issues.

I discovered a free set of radials from a Subaru that match the current tire specifications (205/70R15) and offer higher weight ratings than the existing tires (7.75-15ST). While these aren't trailer-specific tires, they are radials and will allow me to tow for now until I can purchase proper trailer or light truck tires.

I also took some additional photos after driving 8 miles on a gravel road to rest in my yard. Here are the images:

![](full_image)

![](full_image)

![](full_image)

![](full_image)

Inside views: 

![](full_image)

The best part? AM/FM and 8-Track! I’m considering upgrading to a CD player.

I’ve started pulling back some floor panels, but fortunately, the underlying framing is still intact. Additional framing will be added in high-traffic areas for reinforcement.

From an insurance perspective, most companies do not offer fixed-price coverage for such items. Investing significant funds could lead to overvaluation, resulting in a higher investment than the item's actual insurable value.

I did not insure my previous RV, as my insurance agent deemed its value unworthy of coverage. From a liability perspective, my truck insurance would suffice. However, my new Jayco RV is now fully insured.

Yesterday, I pressure-washed the entire trailer, giving it a much cleaner appearance. A few panels need repainting due to sun damage, and all light lenses were cleaned; only one was broken.

Inside, I removed the couch/bed, fresh water tank, and water heater, both of which appear in good condition. I plan to add about a gallon of bleach to the water tank and let it sit in the sun for several weeks.

Structural wood inspection shows solid conditions, though some cheap chipboard subfloor and paneling are damaged. Today, I acquired a set of Republic Enterprise 205/70R15 tires for free; they have about 60% tread left and can hold an additional 150lbs per tire.

With Devin's help, we easily removed and mounted the tires using lumber and a truck to break the beads. The tires are now ready for balancing in the truck.
Great project! Keep us updated on your progress.

We also found our range hood on eBay. It was new and incredibly affordable—less than $20 including shipping and handling, which is about what I'd spend on spray paint and sandpaper for the old one. Here are before-and-after photos from my Picasa album: Jim's Camper Pics

Jim, thanks for sharing the gallery link. I had a productive morning before temperatures rose; I disassembled the brakes, cleaned and relubricated them, and repainted the drums black. The brake shoes were in good condition, and the mechanisms functioned correctly. I also pressure-washed and re-mounted the tires, fitting an old center cap from a 1970s GMC.

The water tank and heater have been removed, revealing the internal components. I plan to remove the remaining fixtures this weekend. Additionally, I made a recent eBay purchase that I think you'll enjoy; click here to view it.
Great job on the camper build, and thanks for sharing the picture of your new shirt. Lee

Today's progress was somewhat slow due to a few hour-long motorcycle rides with my friend. However, I managed to make some headway. The dinette was set up, and I addressed some issues by pulling up a rotted subfloor. Several tears in the aluminum, likely from rocks, were discovered and will need patching to prevent water intrusion.

The right edge of the floor’s 2x2 frame is more deteriorated than expected, so it will be replaced along with a few others. For now, all cushions are stored in the bunk, and other furniture like cabinets and tables are in the garage. This storage setup will likely expand as needed.

Tomorrow, I plan to remove the fridge, oven, and possibly some kitchen cabinets.

More progress has been made on the project. Supplies amounting to a few hundred dollars were acquired from a building supply store. The work includes floor pulling and disassembly, installation of patch panels, and applying JB weld. Some siding was removed, and walls are being supported with jacks. A closeup of the sandwich-style construction is provided.

The floor is now ready for new joists, insulation, and flooring. Daylight can be seen under the existing walls. Additional bracing has been added where plywood panels will butt up against the next section. The first floor panel has been installed.

Click to view full images of each step.
Subscribe. I haven't seen anything quite like this before, but it looks amazing so far! Great job.
Great progress has been made on this project.

Thanks for your help. I plan to complete the floor and restore the space in the next few weeks so I can use it before school starts. Once school begins, I won't have time to work on it. After finishing the floor and addressing additional structural issues, I will focus on fixing some wall panels. The front left wall and the back left corner need the most attention structurally.
This is a cool project. I wish I had the confidence to undertake something similar. I also need an Fort Wayne shirt.

If I had more resources, I would completely disassemble and rebuild the trailer, addressing the flooring, walls, and roof. The components are surprisingly simple to work with. Since purchasing the RV, I've frequently questioned my decision due to its leak issues and associated hidden water damage. While so far I've encountered only minor problems, the back corner appears concerning.
The project sounds exciting and promises to be enjoyable once completed.

Added a brace at the joint of the plywood sheets and moved the seam away from the existing joist, positioning it under the dinette for better coverage. Laid more plywood under the kitchen cabinet and have just a small piece left to add in front of the wheelwell. The final section by the trailer's back, where the bathroom is located and walls are present, will be the most challenging.

No progress last night as I was occupied with homework and household chores. Tonight, I hope to complete the installation by placing the final piece of plywood and work on structural wood in the back wall. I have also ordered several items to replace or repair: a clearance light base and lens, porch light lens, fridge roof vent, water tank roof vents, range hood vent, Butyl putty tape for re-sealing windows, doors, and seams, a large box of screws to replace old ones with the putty tape, an additional table leg, pedestal, and base, as well as towing mirrors for the 88.
